Ten placed peoples root 'marsh'; only nine distinct roman forms come back. Two of them collide.

WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN THE OTHERS. Read the comment above the assertion -- it is the whole story, and it is not mine:

  "THE GRANARY conversion (2026-08-25): this witness pinned WHICH peoples gap
   'marsh' at seed 42 - a world-content snapshot that broke on every campaign
   that moved settlements (FIVE RE-PINS IN THIS FILE'S HISTORY before this
   one). What the pipeline actually guarantees is structural, and that is what
   is asserted now."

Someone already had this argument, in this file, and won it. They replaced a content snapshot with the structural guarantee -- total partition, distinct non-empty roman forms within a concept, non-degenerate both ways -- precisely so that a campaign moving settlements would get a real signal instead of a sixth re-pin. Your campaign moved settlements harder than any of those five, and what broke is not the snapshot. It is the structural guarantee.

AND THERE IS NOTHING TO BUMP. The assertion is `romans.len() == rooted.len()`. That is a set-size identity, not a pinned constant: there is no 10 to change to 9. The only way to make it pass is to weaken the invariant so duplicates are allowed, which deletes the property outright. That is a good test, and it is worth saying so after a night in which several fixtures could be re-anchored.

WHAT I THINK HAPPENED. Your redistribution changed which peoples are PLACED. bugbear +39, human +33, hobgoblin +19, gully-dwarf +16 moved into what kobold, wood-elf and the dwarves vacated. `placed_peoples(&w)` is the test's input, so a people that was not placed at seed 42 before is placed now, and its 'marsh' root duplicates one already there. That is a real consequence of the population change, not a fixture artifact.

WHAT TO DO: name the two. Dump `rooted` and find which pair shares a roman. Then decide whether a shared root between those two specific peoples is acceptable -- it may be, if they are linguistically close -- or whether the lexicon should be producing distinct forms and is not. That is a naming-system question, and it is the first one tonight that is not answerable by looking at the world.
